# University of Melbourne: Overview
Founded in 1853 following proposals from Hugh Childers, the University of Melbourne is Australia's second oldest university, established through an Act of Incorporation with powers to confer degrees in arts, medicine, laws, and music. The university's initial growth was fueled by Victoria's gold rush, with the first classes commencing in 1855 and the first chancellor, Redmond Barry, serving until 1880. Over time, the university expanded its faculties—including Arts, Law, Engineering, Medicine, and residential colleges for all Christian denominations—admitting women beginning in 1881. The university continued to grow throughout the 20th century, weathering economic challenges and developing new courses, research centers, and faculties. The Melbourne Model was introduced in 2008, transitioning undergraduate degrees into a generalist format followed by specialisation in post-graduate study.
Today, the university is comprised of nine major faculties (including Arts, Business and Economics, Education, Engineering and IT, Fine Arts and Music, Law, Medicine, and Science) and is recognized as Australia's top university in several international rankings (QS: #19, THE: #37, ARWU: #38, CWTS Leiden: #36, USNWR: #30). The main Parkville campus is complemented by several metropolitan and regional campuses in Burnley, Southbank, Werribee, Creswick, Dookie, and Shepparton, as well as a new engineering campus under development at Fishermans Bend. The university has a significant research profile, being ranked 29th globally by NTU and 57th by CWUR, and maintains extensive networks of research centers, libraries, museums, and galleries.

# Student Life, Governance, and Notable Alumni
The University of Melbourne supports a vibrant student community through two major student unions (UMSU and GSA) and over 300 student clubs and societies. Sport is overseen by Melbourne University Sport, with several clubs (football, lacrosse, cycling, tennis, rowing) dating back to the 19th century. Residential life is centered around nine affiliated colleges and multiple halls of residence. Admissions are highly competitive (median ATAR 94.05), and 44% of students are international. The university is governed by a Council led by the chancellor, with administrative operations managed by the Vice-Chancellor and executive team. Jane Hansen is the current chancellor, and Emma Johnston is set to become vice-chancellor in 2025—the first woman to hold the role.
The university boasts many notable alumni, including four Australian prime ministers (Alfred Deakin, Harold Holt, Julia Gillard, Robert Menzies), Nobel laureates (Elizabeth Blackburn, Sir James Mirrlees, Frank Macfarlane Burnet, John Eccles, Bert Sakmann, Howard Florey, Joshua Lederberg, Richard Robson), and distinguished figures across diverse fields like Cate Blanchett, Portia de Rossi, Peter Singer, Germaine Greer, Barry Humphries, and David Warren. The University of Melbourne recognizes outstanding contributors with the University of Melbourne Award and has made significant cultural, academic, and scientific impacts both nationally and globally.
